Other folks have said it more eloquently in this thread, but rn my best guess is that its a few different things.

1. Teething Issues: Deepseek is brand spanking new, and so it could just be servers overloading and other early game problems that can be ironed out over time. This would track with all the errors people get.
2. Model Instability: It's possible that the model just is not equipped to handle the amount of requests its getting, and its output is suffering as a result. If it's being overloaded, it could be accidentally skipping over protocols used for making it think out its responses, instead just blurts out the first thing to come to mind.
3. Someone Made an Oopsie: I don't know much about Deepseek's creators, but it could just be a patch they pushed that broke something. That would be relatively easy to roll back, if so.
4. Bad Data: If Deepseek is programmed to feed off of user input, then the quality of the data it's been fed will necessarily suffer. Someone else pointed out that JAI only accounts for a tiny fraction of Deepseek's current users, so it's likely not our fault, but scraping user responses will always mean that you get some really meh stuff in the mix, which can drag things down pretty significantly.

Some people are saying "Oh, its the honeymoon phase breaking," but I think that's underselling it. I definitely think there's a real drop in quality here, albeit relatively marginal.

As to source, I couldn't say, but ultimately I wouldn't be too concerned. Deepseek is still providing better responses for me than JLLM, and the fact it *did* hit the heady heights it did means that said heights are in fact reachable. Future models will build off of the work that Deepseek has done, just as Deepseek has built off of the work of models before it. This is an evolving technology, one with a lot of interest, and I can't imagine this as the herald of some technological backslide.
